content: The key activities for quality control in pathology laboratories must be meticulously performed and monitored. While some reagents and solutions can be commercially purchased, others may need to be prepared in the laboratory following a standardized operating procedure (SOP). Once prepared, bottles must be labeled with the stain name, concentration, preparation date, service start date, expiration date, and the preparer's name. Proper storage at the correct temperature and protection from light are essential. Certain stains can degrade over time, losing their ability to produce accurate reactions. Therefore, daily quality checks using positive and negative control materials, as per a defined SOP, are necessary. Records of staining characteristics should be maintained. Stains should also be regularly inspected for precipitation, crystal formation, or bacterial contamination. The use of high-quality paraffin with an appropriate melting point is critical for tissue impregnation and embedding. An information management system is essential for effective patient data management. This system can be paper-based, partially computerized, or fully computerized. While establishing a computerized laboratory information system requires infrastructure, hardware, software, trained personnel, and utilities, it facilitates timely pathology reporting, supports clinical decision-making, and aids in resource planning. Such systems can function as standalone laboratory systems or be integrated into larger hospital information systems. Accurate disease coding is vital for identifying patterns, such as higher cancer incidences in specific geographic areas or age groups. This information can guide investigations into underlying triggers and their mitigation. Disease coding requires determining whether a specimen is malignant, in situ, benign, or of uncertain histologic behavior. The WHO International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) provides codes for diseases, symptoms, and external causes, while the International Classification of Diseases for Oncology (ICD-O) is the definitive classification for neoplasms. Cancer registries worldwide use ICD-O to record malignancy incidence and survival rates, informing cancer control, research, treatment planning, and health economics. Occurrence management involves identifying and addressing errors or near-errors, forming a critical component of laboratory quality management. Common sources of error include incorrect specimen collection, mislabeling, improper storage, and unsafe transportation. These issues can be mitigated through clinician education and adherence to SOPs. Analytical errors, such as specimen misidentification or loss, require secondary checks, barcode technology, and clear SOPs. Corrective actions aim to prevent error recurrence. External quality assessment (EQA) objectively evaluates laboratory performance through proficiency testing, rechecking slides, and onsite evaluations. EQA promotes professional standards, peer review, and dialogue among pathologists. Laboratories should participate in accredited EQA programs, with a minimum of two pathologists reviewing malignant diagnoses in high-income countries. Telepathology and telemonitoring can provide similar review levels in resource-limited settings. Audits, both internal and external, help laboratories benchmark performance and identify areas for improvement. Internal audits, conducted as needed, enhance staff awareness of quality requirements and prepare for external audits. External audits verify compliance with documented standards. Accreditation, performed by qualified organizations, formally recognizes a laboratory's competence to deliver accurate and reproducible results. Key accreditation requirements include process control, document control, personnel management, health and safety compliance, equipment management, and data management. Process improvement involves continuous enhancement of laboratory quality. Examples of quality indicators include the percentage of suboptimal specimens submitted for diagnosis, turnaround times, and diagnostic discrepancy rates. Corrective actions, such as clinician training and process adjustments, address identified issues. Customer service is a primary goal of pathology laboratories, encompassing patients, physicians, healthcare providers, public health agencies, and the community.
